newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Credit Lyonnais unit to appeal Tapie ruling.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Credit Lyonnais unit to appeal Tapie ruling.

text.p: A former subsidiary of troubled French state bank Credit Lyonnais said on Friday it would appeal a court order condemning it to pay 600 million francs ($120 million) for lending businessmman Bernard Tapie too much money and contributing to his downfall.

"Of course we will appeal," said a spokesman for the rescue vehicle set up under last year's state bailout of Credit Lyonnais that now owns the unit -- Societe de Banque Occidentale (SDBO) -- and many of the bank's other shaky assets.

The Paris commercial court on Thursday sharply criticised the SDBO -- best known as Tapie's banker in the 1980s -- for providing the businessman with "ill-considered and exorbitant" support and ordered it to pay a provisional 600 million francs to the liquidators of his industrial empire.

The SDBO "knew from 1989 the two main companies belonging to Tapie, GBT (Groupe Bernard Tapie) and FIBT (Financiere et immobiliere Bernard Tapie) were in a state of default," the court said. "Not only did SDBO maintain its assistance but it increased it, creating an insurmountable debt," the court said.

The former Socialist minister and soccer boss, who owes Credit Lyonnais 1.2 billion francs, has long maintained the state-owned bank was at least partly responsible for the collapse of his empire because it was involved in running it.
Lawyers for Tapie said on Friday the court ruling was a vindication of his claims. "It's a very nice, very important victory for him," Tapie's lawyer, Bernard Lagarde, told Reuters.
The liquidators filed suit last June against Credit Lyonnais and its former units SDBO and Clinvest, alleging they provided "excessive support" to Tapie.
The court delayed a final ruling on the liquidators' claim for a total 2.5 billion francs in damages and interest to await the outcome of a parallel criminal case.
The former boss of Marseille European soccer champions is now bankrupt and is appealing against prison sentences for match-rigging and business fraud.
Credit Lyonnais, fighting to restore its profitability after a hectic lending spree in the 1980s brought it to the edge of collapse, has denied responsibility for Tapie's troubles.

It no longer has financial responsibility for SDBO and Clinvest. Under a state bailout of Credit Lyonnais in 1995, the units were hived off from the bank and put under the ownership of the state-backed rescue body Consortium de Realisations, which is charged with selling off the bank's bad assets.

The court also ordered a three-man panel of experts to look into the sale of Adidas which was sold off in 1994. Tapie has accused Credit Lyonnais of forcing him to sell a majority stake in Adidas to a group of investors too cheaply and alleges the bank profited unfairly when it sold its holding in Adidas.
Tapie is hoping the liquidators' case will establish that Credit Lyonnais owes him several billion francs from capital gains on the Adidas sale.
